So the book al-Muʿlim consists of lessons which he used to deliver in the congregational mosque during the season of Ramadan, expounding Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim. Some of the students used to write them down, and that was then gathered into this book, the book al-Muʿlim. It has been printed in the edition of Muhammad al-Shadhili al-Nayfar, published by Dar al-Gharb al-Islami, in three volumes. In it are a very great many useful points, together with exact wording — such that if a man reads it he would not suppose it to be a lesson set down from dictation without recourse to books. Those who possess this faculty in the matter of dictation, so that the words they dictate are like the words they write with their own hands, are very few. Many people have their eloquence in their tongues, and many likewise have their eloquence in their pens; those whose eloquence combines the two things, the pen and the tongue, are few. Among them is Imam al-Mazari, and among them likewise is Imam Ibn Daqiq al-ʿId. His commentary on al-ʿUmdah was delivered orally — merely lessons which he dictated from memory — and his commentary on al-Arbaʿīn al-Nawawiyyah was likewise delivered orally, only a lesson; yet if a man reads it he supposes it to be the deliberation of a man writing with his own hand and labouring at it, and especially the extreme concentration of the commentary on al-ʿUmdah, even though it is mere dictation which he dictated from memory.

After al-Mazari came Imam Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Qurtubi al-Andalusi. He abridged Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and divided it into chapters — he made chapter headings for it, because Muslim made books for it but made no chapters for it, unlike al-Bukhari. Al-Bukhari wrote the books and the chapters, whereas Muslim wrote the books in the Ṣaḥīḥ and wrote no chapters. So Imam Abu al-ʿAbbas came and set chapters for the Ṣaḥīḥ, suited to the hadiths which Muslim brings forward; and he abridged it and commented on his own abridgement. His abridgement does not follow the order of the Ṣaḥīḥ: he brings some chapters forward within some of the books and puts others back, according to the connections he himself sees. He commented on it in a commentary which he named al-Mufhim fī Sharḥ Ikhtiṣār Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, and it has been printed.

Then came the judge Abu al-Fadl ʿIyad ibn Musa ibn ʿIyad ibn Musa ibn ʿIyad al-Yahsubi al-Sabti, and he composed Ikmāl al-Muʿlim, by which he completed the book of al-Mazari, so that it came to contain the whole of Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and was a commentary on the entire Ṣaḥīḥ. It is rich in useful points, especially in the juristic field; and the judge, may God have mercy on him, gave attention in it to the transmissions of the Ṣaḥīḥ. The difficulty, however, is that the judge was not a man of travel, so the transmissions current in the East did not reach him — some of them did not reach him, and he would deny their existence, although he denied it with respect to his own country, saying: "There is no transmission of the Ṣaḥīḥ in our country that establishes such-and-such." He was extremely exact, because he memorised Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim as one memorises the Fatihah, and so he was extremely exact in the transmission of it. He wished, may God have mercy on him, to add to his commentary, until he died, God's mercy upon him — the Almohads slaughtered him, for he had been a judge under the Almoravid state. He wished to make additions in certain places in his commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, and for this reason he expanded in commenting on some hadiths, and these were made into independent books, such as his book Bughyat al-Rāʾid li-mā Taḍammanahu Ḥadīth Umm Zarʿ min al-Fawāʾid. On the hadith of Umm Zarʿ alone he composed a book, Bughyat al-Rāʾid, and it is in print. He likewise wished to set down his chains of transmission in the introduction to his book, but they were not set down; they are found in his book al-Ghunyah, which is in print, containing all the chains of ʿIyad.

Then after him came Imam al-Nawawi, Abu Zakariyya Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Dimashqi, may God have mercy on him. He gave the greatest attention to Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and commented on it in a commentary for which God laid down acceptance, so that it became famous and spread through the lands, as al-Nawawi's books did. They are books — glory be to God — upon which God laid a remarkable acceptance, despite what is in them at times of errors, and despite the shortness of the man's life, for he lived only forty-one years. Yet for all that, God laid acceptance upon these books, so that riders carried them into the east of the earth and its west. This book of his, al-Minhāj fī Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj, is a book in which he combined what al-Mazari mentioned and what the judge ʿIyad mentioned, and added to it discussion also of the eastern transmissions of Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim; and for that reason he answers ʿIyad on matters concerning the transmissions. The Hafiz Ibn Hajar gave attention to the matter of the transmissions from the two books in Fatḥ al-Bārī, in the hadiths held in common which al-Bukhari brought out: the Hafiz attends to the words of the judge ʿIyad and the words of al-Nawawi on the transmissions. An example is the hadith of Jaʿfar ibn Mubashshir, in which the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to the bedouin, "He has prospered, by his father, if he is truthful." The judge mentioned that some people transmit it as "He has prospered, by God, if he is truthful," and claim that the original word was "by God" written thus, and that the two lāms were shortened so that some people read it "by his father," since the dots were not attended to. He said: this is void, because the established transmission with us is "He has prospered, by his father, if he is truthful," and there is no transmission of Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim in our country that transmits "by God." The Hafiz, however, mentioned that a transmission of Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim may perhaps have been found in which there is "by God."

Likewise came al-Ubbi, the well-known pupil of Ibn ʿArafah, in what concerns transmitted knowledge. Ibn ʿArafah al-Warghami, the imam of the mosque of ʿUqbah ibn Nafiʿ in Tunis at al-Qayrawan, was an authority in both the rational and the transmitted sciences, and one of the most famous of the Malikis' verifying scholars in that age. But among his pupils were al-Burzuli and al-Ubbi, and he used not to sleep at night. His slave-girl said to him: "What is the matter with you, my master, that you do not sleep?" He said to her: "How shall I sleep when in the morning I shall be between these two ravening lions — between al-Ubbi with his transmitted learning and al-Burzuli with his reasoning?" For the two of them used to dispute with him over every matter; so he would spend the night going over his information, saying: if I say such-and-such in the lesson, al-Ubbi will object with such-and-such, and the answer to him is such-and-such; and al-Burzuli will object with such-and-such, and the answer to him is such-and-such; and the answer to that answer may be such-and-such. He would bring up all the possibilities and answer them, preparing the lesson with exacting preparation. Ibn ʿArafah, may God have mercy on him, was much given to returning to the truth. It is said that he was afflicted with an illness because of lack of sleep, and that this illness was a failure of memory, so that when something of his own notes was set before him he did not understand it, because he had been enamoured of exactness and difficulty of style. For that reason, whoever reads his abridgement in Maliki jurisprudence today understands nothing of it but the rarities; you can hardly understand anything of it. He gave the greatest attention to definitions and technical delimitations, so that when the Malikis wished to define something they would say: Ibn ʿArafah's definition of it, or Ibn ʿArafah's delimitation of it. His delimitations have been gathered and commented upon by al-Rassaʿ in his book Sharḥ Ḥudūd Ibn ʿArafah, which is printed in two volumes. As for al-Ubbi, may God have mercy on him, he completed the book of the judge ʿIyad by adding to it many useful points which the judge had intended to add, and especially in the juristic, creedal and spiritual fields; and he set out in it investigations in legal theory as well. So his book was among the most important of books. He would use symbols for the earlier books — each of the commentaries on Muslim he designates by a particular symbol, a letter — and he named his book Ikmāl Ikmāl al-Muʿlim: for the judge named his book Ikmāl al-Muʿlim, and this man named his Ikmāl al-Ikmāl.

Then after him came al-Sanusi, who died in the year 1040 of the Hijrah — a late figure. He composed his book Takmilat Ikmāl Ikmāl al-Muʿlim, in which he gathered the useful points al-Nawawi had added and added to them further, and gave attention also to the principles of jurisprudence and to theology (ʿilm al-kalām), adding that to his book.

Al-Suyuti composed a brief book on Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim which he named al-Dībāj fī Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj. It exists in manuscript in a single small volume, and it has now been printed in several parts, even though it exists in abridged form in a notebook — a small notebook, glory be to God, the manuscript.

For all this, Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim has remained in need, down to the present, of some service. The ancients felt Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim's need of service, so much so that Ibn al-Salah composed on it the book Ṣiyānat Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim ʿan al-Ghalaṭ wa-l-Taḥrīf wa-l-Taṣḥīf. This book has been printed on its own, and it has also been printed together with Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim in that edition which is in one volume: the book Ṣiyānat Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim… is printed with it.

Likewise, the fourth of the hadith books to which attention has been given in commentary is the book Sunan Abī Dāwūd. It has already been said that al-Khattabi commented on it, but he did not attend to the transmissions of the Sunan. Of the transmissions of the Sunan that became well known, the two most famous are the transmission of al-Luʾluʾi and the transmission of Ibn Dasah — these are the most famous transmissions of Sunan Abī Dāwūd — and between them is plain divergence, even in the placing of hadiths earlier or later, and in grading them sound or weak, and in the rulings which Abu Dawud brings after them. For that reason there is need to combine these differing recensions; and al-Khattabi did not attend to that. Indeed he did not comment on all the hadiths in Sunan Abī Dāwūd.

Al-Mundhiri abridged Sunan Abī Dāwūd as he abridged Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, and Ibn al-Qayyim commented on al-Mundhiri's abridgement. He too, it appears, did not intend to comment on the whole book; rather he intended to write notes and useful remarks on it, expanding in some investigations and passing over and turning aside from many hadiths on which he says nothing.

Wali Allah al-Dihlawi, who is the author of the hadith revival in India, gave attention to commenting on it; he gave the greatest attention to Sunan Abī Dāwūd. What is regrettable, however, is that the commentaries he wrote on it were all lost, and nothing of them has reached us; they were plundered in the days of his son Ismaʿil. His son grieved over the loss of these books, and so he ordered some of his students to give attention to gathering copies of the Sunan of Abu Dawud. They gathered a large number of them and collated them, so that the copy they had was one against which the divergences of the transmissions were collated; and upon it is the commentary of the author of ʿAwn al-Maʿbūd. The old Indian printing of ʿAwn al-Maʿbūd therefore contains the divergences of the transmissions in Sunan Abī Dāwūd. The trouble, however, is that the presses found this divergence of transmissions burdensome and deleted it in the new printings, because they are not students of knowledge and do not suppose there is any benefit in it, so they deleted it. For that reason this Indian printing is now exhausted in the markets; it is practically not to be found for sale in the Arab lands, and it contains very great benefits in the divergence of the recensions.

The Indians gave attention to Sunan Abī Dāwūd and wrote a number of commentaries on it, among them Badhl al-Majhūd — in addition to ʿAwn al-Maʿbūd, of course — but ʿAwn al-Maʿbūd is the best and most important of them, and its author is one of these later Indians who were influenced by the revival which Wali Allah al-Dihlawi set up.

Al-Suyuti likewise commented on Sunan Abī Dāwūd in a curtailed commentary, after his own custom. Like it is al-Sindi's gloss on it, just as he has glosses on all six books: a gloss on Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, printed; a gloss on Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, not printed; a gloss on Sunan Abī Dāwūd, printed; a gloss on Sunan al-Nasāʾī, printed; a gloss on Sunan al-Tirmidhī, not printed; and a gloss on Sunan Ibn Mājah, printed. His gloss on Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī was printed, and his gloss on Abu Dawud, and his gloss on al-Nasaʾi, and his gloss on Ibn Majah.

Sunan Abī Dāwūd still stands in need of commentaries and attention; and for that reason the printings of it which exist, to which we have pointed before, contain much plain divergence. The best of them is the printing of ʿUbayd al-Daʿʿas and his colleagues — ʿIzzat ʿUbayd al-Daʿʿas — and there is a printing which Muhyi al-Din ʿAbd al-Hamid edited, or rather corrected, in the matter of vocalisation only, because Muhyi al-Din ʿAbd al-Hamid is not a hadith scholar but a linguist and grammarian, so that his work in it goes no further than fixing the words and vowelling those that need vowelling.

Then there is Sunan al-Tirmidhī, which Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi commented upon in his book ʿĀriḍat al-Aḥwadhī. The ʿāriḍah is the light, hidden wing, and the aḥwadhī is the small eagle that ranges far in flight through the air; the eagle's wing is likewise called aḥwadhī — so aḥwadhī is the eagle, and its wing as well. From this are the words of the poet:

*Upon two swift pinions she rose at evening, and she was no more than a glimpse, and then she is gone.*

What Ibn al-ʿArabi, may God have mercy on him, intended is that his book is only a wing, and that he did not intend by it to cover the whole book. He brought into it many useful points and sciences, but the trouble is that it has not been printed in an adequate printing: all the printings of it that exist contain errors known only to God — omission and dropping out, and the most extreme corruption of the text. When he brings forward the hadith he says: this hadith contains five juristic questions, three creedal questions and two questions of legal theory; then, when you examine the questions, you find only two juristic questions and one creedal question — and so on: a complete disfigurement. Yet for all that, in what is printed of it there are very great benefits, and in it are many questions to be found nowhere else.

Among the good commentaries on Sunan al-Tirmidhī is the book al-Nafḥ al-Shadhī by the Hafiz Ibn Sayyid al-Nas. It exists complete in manuscript, and Dr Ahmad Maʿbad has edited three volumes of it, in which only thirteen hadiths appeared, because he is remarkably long in the matter of documentation (takhrīj).

Al-Mubarakfuri likewise commented on it in his book Tuḥfat al-Aḥwadhī, which is a good book. He gave excellent attention in it to documentation and to jurisprudence, and relied in juristic documentation upon Naṣb al-Rāyah of al-Zaylaʿi. He also gave attention to the lines of transmission, and especially to what al-Hakim brings forward of them in al-Mustadrak and what al-Bayhaqi brings forward in al-Sunan al-Kubrā and in Maʿrifat al-Sunan wa-l-Āthār. So his book is generally useful. But Sunan al-Tirmidhī is a sea without a shore, for several reasons; and whoever wishes to teach it or to comment on it needs these things:

First, he needs a comparison of the recensions, because of their divergence in the grading, for al-Tirmidhi in some recensions says "sound" (ṣaḥīḥ), in some "good" (ḥasan), in some "good, sound," and in some "good, sound, rare" — all upon one and the same hadith. This divergence, in the exact determination of that grading alone, deserves a great labour.

The other matter is that al-Tirmidhi's book is drawn out upon the two Ṣaḥīḥs, and for that reason, when a hadith is famous in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, he brings it forward by a line other than the line of the two Ṣaḥīḥs and then says, "and in the chapter there are reports from so-and-so and so-and-so" among the Companions. So you need to know the hadiths folded away to which he is pointing. Some of the earlier scholars composed works on them — al-Lubāb fī Qawl al-Tirmidhī fī al-Bāb — Ibn al-Mulaqqin and others composed on them; but none of these is in our hands today, and al-Mubarakfuri did not give them sufficient attention. The printed recensions of Sunan al-Tirmidhī are likewise of unequal quality. Shaykh Ahmad Shakir, God's mercy upon him, wished to bring out a correct recension of Sunan al-Tirmidhī after his own custom of exactness in publication, but he wrote only two volumes of it, and death came upon him before he completed it. After him came Muhammad Fuʾad ʿAbd al-Baqi, who wished to set one part right; he at least numbered its hadiths and its chapters in accordance with what is in al-Tuḥfah of al-Mizzi, but he is not able to grade or to document as Abu al-Ashbal did, and he did that for one volume only. The trouble is that the publishing houses wished to complete the book and entrusted it to someone not fit for that. So it was printed in two printings, one of them with the completion by ʿAtiyyah ʿAwad ʿAtwah, and in this there is an astonishing abundance of errors. Among the marvels reported of him is that, for example, at the mention of the hadith, "The woman inherits from her foundling, from her freed slave, and from her child over whom she performed the oath of imprecation," he put a reference number on it and wrote beneath, "al-ʿanat means hardship" — the trouble being that in the body of the text the wording is correct: he did not write lā ʿanata ʿalayhi ("there is no hardship upon him"), but wrote lāʿanat ʿalayhi ("she performed the oath of imprecation concerning him"). This sort of stupidity is most remarkable. Following in his track, too, is the second man who came after him in this, Yusuf Kamal al-Hut, who set down the errors as they were and added other errors to them. The edition of ʿIzzat al-Daʿʿas is better than this one and that one; and would that he had brought in the useful matter which Shakir brought in the first two parts, the first and the second — but he did not do so. Bashshar ʿAwwad then brought out a recension of it in which he left aside recourse to many manuscripts and neglected recourse to the printed editions as well; but at least it is a recension sound in itself and in its form, and the errors found in al-Hut and in ʿAtiyyah ʿAtwah he did not bring forward. He did, however, neglect much of what al-Daʿʿas brought forward — for instance the comparison of the handwritten recensions.

After this is the book Sunan al-Nasāʾī, and attention given to this book is slight on the side of commentary. I know of no commentary on it by the early scholars. The first whose commentary on it has reached us is al-Suyuti, and his commentary is after al-Suyuti's custom; then al-Sindi, who has a gloss on it printed together with al-Suyuti's commentary. Shaykh Muhammad al-Mukhtar ibn Ahmad Mazid wished to comment on it; he used to teach it in the Mosque of the Prophet in Medina, and he commented on a small number of its hadiths in three parts. He expanded, because he expands in documentation and on the juristic side; then death came upon him before he completed it — the father of Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Mukhtar, the man who now teaches in the Sanctuary. Nor was the book given sufficient attention here either; it still stands in need of being commented upon and attended to.

As for Sunan Ibn Mājah, al-Busiri gave it attention long ago, but his attention to it was confined to its additions alone — the hadiths it adds beyond the other five books — and Miṣbāḥ al-Zujājah by al-Busiri has been printed. Muhammad Fuʾad ʿAbd al-Baqi, in his recension of Sunan Ibn Mājah, abridged al-Busiri's grading of the additions, so that he writes on the additions such-and-such at the foot of the hadith. Likewise there is al-Sindi's gloss on it and al-Suyuti's commentary, and it has not been given sufficient attention. Ibn Qutlubugha commented on it, but his is an abridgement as well and there is not enough in it, and the book still stands in need of attention even now. For this reason the recensions in circulation today — those printed of it — contain errors. The best of them is the recension of Fuʾad ʿAbd al-Baqi; and there is Bashshar's recension as well, this new one; and before it the recension of al-Aʿzami, in which there are gross errors. At present Husayn ibn Nasir al-Hakami is attempting to serve the book: he has gathered a great deal of information about it and has examined many of the recensions, but he has not brought out anything in print to this day.

As for the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, it has not been favoured with many commentaries, because in the lifetime of its author, and the lifetime of his son, and the lifetime of Abu Bakr al-Qatiʿi, it was confined in transmission to a single person in each generation, and for that reason it was not given sufficient attention — although various people composed books relating to it which serve certain aspects of it, such as the arranging of the Companions in the Musnad by Ibn al-Jawzi, and such as al-Qawl al-Musaddad fī al-Dhabb ʿan Musnad al-Imām Aḥmad, answering Ibn al-Jawzi himself when he mentioned certain hadiths which he claimed were forged though they are in the Musnad. So the Hafiz Ibn Hajar defended it with this book. Al-Suyuti likewise defends it in his book which he named al-Qawl al-Ḥasan fī al-Dhabb ʿan Jamīʿ al-Sunan, in which he also took up everything that Ibn al-Jawzi claimed was forged while it is in the Sunan, or in the Musnad, or in the Mustadrak.

Shaykh Ahmad Shakir, God's mercy upon him, attempted to bring the book out in a satisfactory form, and twenty-two volumes of it were printed, containing roughly a quarter of the book; he reached roughly the middle of the second part, or a little more, and then died before completing it. In general, what he did serve of the Musnad, his service in it was noble and evident. The book has not been served by any other adequate service: Shaykh al-Saʿati al-Banna, God's mercy upon him, arranged the book on the arrangement of the disciplines, taking it out of the manner of a Musnad, as was his custom — for he did this also with the book Musnad al-Ṭayālisī in Minḥat al-Maʿbūd — and he likewise arranged the Musnad of Imam Ahmad in his book al-Fatḥ al-Rabbānī fī Tartīb Musnad al-Imām Aḥmad al-Shaybānī. He attempted to comment on some of the hadiths in it, but did not cover the commentary on the book; and the commentary also brings in Imam Ahmad's chain of transmission, because he gives the hadiths first stripped of their chains and then brings the chains in the commentary. Generally speaking, the book still stands in need of noble service. The project of editing it has begun — the one of which thirty volumes are now printed, under the supervision of Shaykh Shuʿayb al-Arnaʾut; may God bring it to completion in good.

Likewise al-Mustadrak of al-Hakim: it was given no attention in the author's own time, and the first to give it attention, in roughly the fullest degree, was Imam al-Dhahabi. He abridged it in an abridgement in which he criticises al-Hakim's grading of the hadiths. His method in the abridgement was not regular: he passes over many of the hadiths and the gradings in silence although he does not agree with al-Hakim in his grading of them; and likewise he deletes al-Hakim's chain of transmission from its beginning and gives the chain from the middle, cutting the chain short after al-Mizzi's manner in al-Tuḥfah — roughly. It has been printed in the margin of al-Mustadrak, and there is no commentary on it; only the attention which al-Dhahabi gave it in the abridgement, where he said: "I hope that God will appoint for this book one of the accomplished students of knowledge to complete this work" — and to this day that has not been found. Shaykh Mahmud is attempting to bring the book out and edit it, but we have seen nothing appear as yet.

As for the Sunan of al-Bayhaqi, Ibn Qutlubugha gave it attention and composed his book al-Jawhar al-Naqī on the Sunan of al-Bayhaqi, which is a very brief gloss, in which he is concerned to answer al-Bayhaqi whenever he differs from Abu Hanifah; when he differs from the Hanafis he assails him, and that alone. For that reason this is not sufficient to serve the book. Among those who gave the book attention — in memorisation, study and teaching — was Imam al-Nawawi; and we would have wished that al-Nawawi, may God have mercy on him, had commented on it. Hence he mentioned in al-Taqrīb that among the things a student of knowledge ought to attend to and expend his effort upon is the book of al-Bayhaqi. All the authorities on hadith terminology mention this: when they mention the library of the hadith scholar they seal it with the book of al-Bayhaqi, and they praise it with fragrant praise. Even so, the book still stands in need of service.

Among the books that have been commented upon and to which people have given attention in commentary is the book Mishkāt al-Maṣābīḥ by al-Tibrizi, which is an abridgement of al-Maṣābīḥ by al-Baghawi. The later scholars gave it attention and set several commentaries upon it, among them Mirqāt al-Mafātīḥ and Mirʿāt al-Mafātīḥ, both of them on Mishkāt al-Maṣābīḥ; and al-Tibi's commentary, earlier than these, on the Mishkāt, is printed. Likewise among the hadith books to which people have given attention in commentary are the books of legal rulings. For example the book Muntaqā al-Akhbār by ʿAbd al-Salam ibn Taymiyyah was commented upon by Imam al-Shawkani in a masterly commentary, Nayl al-Awṭār, in which he was original and excellent — except that in the book there are many errors, going back either to a deficiency of references or to corruption in them; and some of them may be printers' errors and not from al-Shawkani, may God have mercy on him. Often, for example, Sulayman al-Nakhaʿi is confused in it with Sulayman al-Taymi, or Malik ibn Anas with Malik ibn Dinar. The book needs attention; yet withal a great effort was expended upon it, and it is now a reference among the references for the commentaries on the books of rulings — among the most important of them, or rather it is the most important of them outright, roughly speaking.

Likewise the book al-ʿUmdah by the Hafiz al-Maqdisi: Ibn Daqiq al-ʿId commented on it by dictation, and his commentary is printed and available — the commentary on al-ʿUmdah by Ibn Daqiq al-ʿId. One of the Maghribis also commented on it in an extensive commentary; this commentary is not extant, but al-Amir al-Sanʿani summarised it in his gloss on al-ʿUmdah. Likewise Bulūgh al-Marām has been commented upon by a number of commentators, and the one that spread and became famous is the book of al-Amir al-Sanʿani upon it, which is Subul al-Salām. It is a book in which he intended to assign the rulings to the schools without expanding on the hadith side; he attended to the juristic side without expanding on the side of hadith criticism. He completes the documentation beyond what the Hafiz Ibn Hajar said; but when the Hafiz points to a hidden defect or the like, he does not pursue it exhaustively. In jurisprudence he gave attention to the doctrines of the Zaydis. It is an abridgement of the Maghribi's commentary upon it in what concerns the jurisprudence of the Sunni schools, but he added to it much of Zaydi jurisprudence that the Maghribi had not brought; and in it too are some errors, which may arise from a lack of acquaintance with many of the doctrines of the people of the Sunnah in the juristic field.

Likewise the book al-Aḥkām al-Wusṭā by the Hafiz ʿAbd al-Haqq al-Ishbili: Imam Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Qattan composed upon it his book Bayān al-Wahm wa-l-Īhām. This book is purely one of hadith criticism: he speaks within the hadith craft, making observations upon ʿAbd al-Haqq ibn al-Kharrat al-Ishbili, may God have mercy on him, regarding his gradings, his selections and his identification of hidden defects. It is a book of hidden defects and documentation, of comparisons between hadiths and the reconciling of divergent ones, and in it are large investigations of hadith terminology. For that reason the Hafiz Ibn Hajar relied upon it in many places: he relies upon Ibn al-Qattan al-Fasi in many matters relating to hidden defects or relating to terminology — and al-Dhahabi likewise.

As for the comprehensive books in hadith, among them for instance is Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn by Imam al-Nawawi, which a number of people have commented upon in middling commentaries, among which there is no distinguished commentary.

This much concerning the commentaries on hadith; and it shows us the importance of this science and of attending to it, and that whoever wishes to occupy himself with knowledge must have an acquaintance with these commentaries and must attempt to combine them, and especially in the hadiths which a number of authors bring out in their books, so that the commentary upon them is multiple.

We forgot, among the important books in the commentaries on hadith in the field of legal rulings, the book Ṭarḥ al-Tathrīb Sharḥ al-Taqrīb. The Hafiz al-ʿIraqi began it and then died before completing it, and his son Abu Zurʿah completed it; and it is a richly furnished book as well. Its first part he devoted to the commentary on the hadith "Deeds are only by intentions" — a whole part on the commentary on this hadith. Others have commented on this hadith in extended commentaries, the most important of them the book of al-Suyuti, Muntahā al-Āmāl fī Sharḥ Ḥadīth Innamā al-Aʿmāl. Al-ʿIraqi mentioned in the commentary a hundred and thirty questions derived from this hadith, and al-Suyuti brought forward in it more than two hundred questions derived from this hadith. Al-Suyuti's book is in print, and Ṭarḥ al-Tathrīb likewise is printed and in circulation. Likewise Fatḥ al-Qadīr bi-Sharḥ al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr by al-Munawi, which is neither expansive nor comprehensive either; rather it attends to the juristic questions and the questions of spiritual conduct, and there is in it no great attention to correcting al-Suyuti's gradings — for many of al-Suyuti's gradings did not have sufficient grounds behind them, and especially when he graded as sound certain hadiths that do not deserve that rank.

In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate.

Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds, and may God bless and grant peace to our Prophet Muhammad and to his family and all his Companions. Among the sciences of the Sunnah that likewise serve it is the science of documentation (takhrīj). It is an important science because it requires two things:

The first: knowing the grading of hadiths as sound or as weak.

The second: knowing what additional wording is in them that may affect the grading.

The earliest generations had no need of this science, and for that reason they did not devise it; it was needed only after the writings on hadith had grown extensive, and many of them were lengthy books which people found hard to transmit with chains — indeed transmission from memory diminished at that point — and so documentation was needed.

Let us begin with the ten preliminaries of the science of documentation, and say:

Its definition: "It is the setting out of who brought the hadith or the report out, and the setting out of its place in the book, and the mention of the grading upon it." So it is a science that takes up three matters:

First: setting out who among the people of knowledge brought the hadith out.

Second: setting out its place, or its places, in the book, because a single hadith may occur in a book several times — al-Bukhari, for instance, brought out one hadith in the Ṣaḥīḥ twenty-two times, and brought out a number of hadiths eighteen times, in different places in the Ṣaḥīḥ.

Third: the grading upon it, either by way of transmission — that you know who among the earlier people of knowledge who specialise in this graded it — or that you yourself attempt, to the extent of your effort, to arrive at a settled conviction about it. This conviction will be a matter of independent reasoning: it may be agreed with and it may be disagreed with, like the conviction that arises for a jurist in a newly arising question. For that reason, if you find a grading upon a hadith as sound or as weak, that does not mean that the matter concerning it is closed; rather it is like your finding a legal opinion of one of the muftis: you may agree with it and you may not. You look at the evidence; and if the conviction arises in you, well and good, you agree; and if it does not arise in you, then you are required to search anew.

As for its subject matter: it is hadiths and reports — that is, the hadiths raised to the Prophet, and the reports halted at the Companions, and likewise the severed ones from the Successors and those who came after them; and the aspect under which they are investigated is the aspect of mentioning their places and of grading them.

Its founder: no definite founder is known for it. Rather, among the famous men who gave attention to the science of documentation is Imam al-Daraqutni, and after him likewise al-Hakim, then al-Bayhaqi, then after him al-Baghawi; then came the champion of this science, al-Zaylaʿi. That was after many jurists had come to rely on weak hadiths and to insert them in their books, so that it became confused, for the non-specialist student of jurisprudence, what is a sound proof and what is not. Here, then, documentation is needed — and especially if you find a book loaded with proofs, for one who is not a student of knowledge finds "the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said," and the custom is that the people of hadith do not say this except for what is certainly sound. These juristic books are stripped of chains of transmission, and their authors also do not for the most part attend to documenting the hadiths; and it is rare for them to say "so-and-so brought it out" — they apply that only to what is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, and this in the first place ought not to need documenting, since people have continued to memorise and transmit the two Ṣaḥīḥs.

So al-Zaylaʿi was the beginning of the closing of this gap, and he composed his book Naṣb al-Rāyah fī Takhrīj Aḥādīth al-Hidāyah. Al-Hidāyah is al-Marghinani's commentary on his own book Bidāyat al-Mubtadī fī al-Fiqh al-Ḥanafī, and in it is a large number of hadiths and reports by which the Hanafis argue; for that reason many of the Hanafi scholars used to suppose that everything in it is sound, whether of the juristic matter or of the hadiths or of the reports.

Its author gave it the greatest attention and combined in it two books from among the books of the Hanafis: the book al-Kitāb, that is, the Mukhtaṣar of al-Quduri — for when the Hanafis say "the Book" without qualification it is that which they mean — and the book al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr by Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani. For the most part he gives their wording and then adds the proofs beyond that. Hence one of the Hanafis said of it:

*Truly al-Hidāyah, like the Qur'an, has abrogated what they composed before it of books in the Law.*

*So keep its rules and keep its useful points, and your speech will be safe from deviation and from falsehood.*

For this reason they gave it great attention and commented upon it with many commentaries. Al-Zaylaʿi, may God have mercy on him, was granted success in confining the hadiths and reports of the book, documenting them and grading them. The grading intended here in documentation is the grading of the hadith as sound or as weak, and not merely the grading of the chain of transmission — for that belongs to the hadith craft. Documentation is nearer to the science of signification than to the science of transmission; documentation is connected with a stage among the stages of the science of comprehension (dirāyah): once you know its soundness, you then derive the useful points from it.

Al-Zaylaʿi, may God have mercy on him, was moderate in his gradings and displayed remarkable skill in the books of hadith. Even so, agreement with his school may drag him into weakening certain hadiths that are in one of the two Ṣaḥīḥs, such as the hadith of "judgment by one witness together with an oath," which is in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas and has come from a number of the Companions — for it has been transmitted from the hadith of Jabir, of Anas, of Abu Hurayrah, of ʿAʾishah and others. The ground of his weakening it lies in two defects. One of them: that Ibn Jurayj, who transmitted it from Sayf ibn ʿUmar from Ibn Shihab, said in it: "I met Ibn Shihab and asked him about it, and he denied it" — and he praised Sayf ibn ʿUmar. So Ibn Shihab did not recall what he had transmitted and denied it, and even so praised Sayf ibn ʿUmar. This does not weaken the hadith, because a transmitter's forgetting what he transmitted, when it has been transmitted from him and a trustworthy man has transmitted it, is a thing that occurs and occurs often, and so it is no impugning of him. Hence Suhayl ibn Abi Salih used to relate from Sufyan from himself: "Sufyan related to me from myself from my father" — because he had forgotten the hadith after he had related it to Sufyan, and so he used to transmit it from Sufyan from himself.

The second defect is that it is an addition to the text, because the Hanafis hold that an addition to the text is abrogation absolutely. God Most High mentioned the instruments of proof in His words: {And call to witness two witnesses from among your men; and if there are not two men, then a man and two women from among such witnesses as you approve} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:282). He made the quorum either two witnesses or a man and two women; and the hadith added a witness and an oath. So they said: this is an addition to the text, and an addition to the text is abrogation, and the Qur'an cannot be abrogated by a solitary report that has a hidden defect. But the answer to this is that this addition is not an addition to the text that abrogates, because the Qur'an did not come in this verse to confine the instruments of proof. The Hanafis agree upon the oath in other than this place and make it an instrument of proof; and this indicates that what is mentioned in the verse is the quorum of testimony only — it confines the quorum of testimony, in other than fornication, to what is mentioned. As for the instruments of proof, the verse did not undertake to confine them: among them is acknowledgement, which is stronger than testimony by agreement; and among them likewise is the writing which God mentioned before this, and the pledge which He mentioned before this. The instruments of proof are many.

Likewise, among the champions of this art is the jurist of the Hanbalis, Ibn Rajab, may God have mercy on him. He had a long reach in hadith and a great skill in its hidden defects, and he received that from the pupils of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, who imparted this skill to them. He composed works in documentation and documented many hadiths, either in small treatises or in some of the books he attended to. Before him likewise is the attention of Shaykh al-Islam, may God have mercy on him, to the documentation of the hadiths by which he argues in particular; but these were not independent books. In fact al-Zaylaʿi had been preceded in documenting by this firm method with clear landmarks in the book al-Tanqīḥ, and for that reason he relies on it much: he relies much on al-Tanqīḥ and quotes from it.

Then after al-Zaylaʿi came the Hafiz Ibn Hajar, who was the master of the people of the science of hadith in his time in the various hadith sciences, among them the science of documentation. He composed a book in which he abridged al-Zaylaʿi's book: the book Naṣb al-Rāyah he abridged in the book al-Bidāyah fī Ikhtiṣār Takhrīj Aḥādīth al-Hidāyah. He likewise documented the hadiths of Sharḥ Fatḥ al-ʿAzīz fī Sharḥ al-Wajīz by al-Rafiʿi, which is the large commentary on al-Wajīz by al-Ghazali. Al-Ghazali composed three books in Shafiʿi jurisprudence — we shall mention them, God willing, under jurisprudence — al-Basīṭ, al-Wasīṭ and al-Wajīz. In al-Wajīz he gives the proofs in brief and points also to the four schools, and so it was the most important of these books. The Shafiʿis gave it much attention, and among those who did so was al-Rafiʿi, who composed three commentaries on it: a long commentary, which is the one called Fatḥ al-ʿAzīz and is now in print; a middling commentary; and a short commentary. This Fatḥ al-ʿAzīz the Shafiʿis attended to greatly, so that al-Fayyumi composed al-Miṣbāḥ al-Munīr fī Gharīb Lughat al-Rāfiʿī al-Kabīr, on what concerns its language; and the Hafiz Ibn Hajar likewise composed Talkhīṣ al-Ḥabīr fī Takhrīj Aḥādīth al-Rāfiʿī al-Kabīr. In this book the Hafiz rendered great service to the proofs for legal rulings, and weakened much that had been a decisive argument with many of the jurists who preceded him. For this reason we have certain hadiths that were relied upon in a stage of jurisprudence before the science of documentation had spread, and upon which was built what may be described as a consensus, while in fact, from the standpoint of the hadith craft, they are weak — such as the hadith "Every loan that brings a benefit is usury," and such as "the hadith of the prohibition of deferred against deferred," and others among the hadiths that are weak from the standpoint of the craft, but upon which consensus took place for centuries past, so that the argument in them became the consensus.

Before the Hafiz Ibn Hajar — as we passed over — came his teacher Abu al-Fadl ʿAbd al-Rahim ibn al-Husayn al-ʿIraqi, who documented the hadiths of Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn in his book al-Mughnī ʿan Ḥaml al-Asfār fī al-Asfār. He took pains, may God Most High have mercy on him, to seek out al-Ghazali's references, which are very many, because God granted al-Ghazali a remarkable opening in memorisation, and in acquaintance likewise, owing to his many travels and the lands in which he settled. So the tracking down of his references was a most laborious matter, and they are many volumes — that is, many tomes. So al-ʿIraqi wished to gather this book so that it might dispense one from carrying the tomes on one's travels.

Al-Suyuti came after the Hafiz Ibn Hajar and was likewise the champion of documentation in his time. Before him, among the famous documenters, was Imam al-Zarkashi, who composed his book al-Muʿtabar fī Takhrīj Aḥādīth al-Minhāj wa-l-Mukhtaṣar — the Minhāj of al-Baydawi and the Mukhtaṣar of Ibn al-Hajib, both of them in the principles of jurisprudence, one of them the standard work of the Malikis and the second the standard work of the Shafiʿis: the Mukhtaṣar of Ibn al-Hajib is the standard work of the Malikis, and the Minhāj of al-Baydawi is the standard work of the Shafiʿis.

Al-Suyuti came and abridged the documentations of al-Zarkashi, al-ʿIraqi and Ibn Hajar in many of the books, and composed his book Takhrīj Aḥādīth al-ʿAqīdah, and the documentation of the hadiths of al-Minhāj, and the documentation of the hadiths of al-Mukhtaṣar, and the documentation of the hadiths of exegesis — and this we mentioned under the science of exegesis, and it is the book al-Durr al-Manthūr — and the documentation of the hadiths of grammar, the hadiths by which the grammarians argue.

Al-Suyuti, may God have mercy on him, gave great attention to documentation, and that on account of the long reach he had in what he had seen of books.

Then documentation remained for a period after these men with nothing new produced in it; and in this age of ours people have returned to documentation. Among those who had the merit of that, after God Most High, is Shaykh Muhammad Nasir al-Din al-Albani, may God have mercy on him. In his period of study he attended to al-ʿIraqi's book al-Mughnī ʿan Ḥaml al-Asfār fī al-Asfār, which is the first book of the books of documentation that fell into his hands, and he attended to it; then afterwards he found the book of Muhammad Murtada al-Zabidi in documenting the hadiths of the Iḥyāʾ as well. So from these two books he learned documentation; he is in documentation a pupil of the book of the Hafiz al-ʿIraqi and of the book of Shaykh Muhammad Murtada al-Zabidi. He composed many books in documentation, some of which may truly be called a composition, because they are ordered and organised books in which he followed the rules of documentation; and some of which are only articles about hadiths that were gathered and do not have the value of composed works. Among the books that truly have the value of a composed work is the book Irwāʾ al-Ghalīl, by which he intended the documentation of the hadiths of Manār al-Sabīl fī Sharḥ al-Dalīl. He was granted success in documenting many of them, even though it was an early beginning — at that time he had not yet mastered many of the hadith rules, nor many of the names of the transmitters and the gradings upon them; and also many of the books had not been sufficiently circulated, and he goes back to a single manuscript which may have a lacuna in it and may have a deficiency in it. For that reason many errors occurred to him in it, from which he later retracted.

As for the books that are not composed in the true sense of composition, they are such as his book Ṣaḥīḥ al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr, and such as his books on Ṣaḥīḥ Sunan Abī Dāwūd and its Ḍaʿīf, and Ṣaḥīḥ Sunan al-Tirmidhī and its Ḍaʿīf, and Ṣaḥīḥ Sunan al-Nasāʾī and its Ḍaʿīf, and Ṣaḥīḥ Sunan Ibn Mājah and its Ḍaʿīf; and such as the series: Silsilat al-Aḥādīth al-Ṣaḥīḥah and Silsilat al-Aḥādīth al-Ḍaʿīfah. These are only articles about hadiths, and for that reason many of them are referrals back to his earlier books, to al-Irwāʾ and others.

In general, God brought benefit through his occupying himself with documentation, so that many researchers followed his track in it and the universities gave attention to it. It was of God's favour upon him that he was appointed to teach in the Islamic University at the beginning of its founding in Medina; and Medina at that time had in it a large number of great and eminent scholars, and also a fair number of men of high resolve among the students of knowledge, who are now among those pointed out with the finger and have in fact become men with schools of their own. These men spread al-Albani's idea of reviving the science of documentation, and for that reason Shaykh al-Albani may be described in this age of ours as the master of "the school of documentation." But one does not say, for instance, the master of "the school of hadith," or the master of "the science of hadith." The hadith sciences are many, and in many of them he had no hand at all, and in many of them his hand was like that of others, or there is among his contemporaries one who is better than he in that. But in documentation he truly gave much benefit, may God have mercy on him; we ask God to accept that from him. Those who followed him in this likewise differed remarkably in their levels. Among those who truly followed the scholarly method in documentation are a few individuals, among them, for instance, Abu Ishaq al-Huwayni in some of his documentations: truly you find the documentation of a verifying scholar, one who has studied documentation and followed in it a path that is not bad. His documentation, for instance, of the book of Ibn al-Jarud is exact documentation.

Among those who were contemporary with al-Albani and profited by his experience, even if they were not his pupils but perhaps had precedence over him in other sciences, is Shaykh Shuʿayb al-Arnaʾut, and there is no doubt that he too is well versed in documentation; and likewise Muhammad ʿAbd Allah al-Siddiq al-Ghumari al-Tanji (northern Morocco). Besides these, the famous men who bring out books today are many.

As for the benefit of the science of documentation, it is — as we mentioned — one of two benefits: the grading of a hadith so as to derive rulings from it. In this benefit there is a discussion which al-Shawkani, may God have mercy on him, raised: namely that many of the imams grade a hadith as weak and then afterwards mention some of its useful points. Among those from whom this occurred is the Hafiz Ibn Hajar himself, and he was preceded in this by a number of the great, such as Ibn ʿAbd al-Hadi the Hanbali and others, and Ibn al-Mulaqqin: they grade a hadith as weak and then say, and there is derived from it "such-and-such." Their intention in that is mental exercise in derivation, and that the weakness of the hadith may be repaired from another quarter. For this reason the method of Shaykh al-Amir al-Sanʿani, may God have mercy on him, of transmitting the weakening of a hadith and then mentioning afterwards what is derived from it, follows this same road. And al-Shawkani, although he criticised this, practised it too: in al-Fawāʾid al-Majmūʿah he criticises it and then acts upon it elsewhere, in Nayl al-Awṭār.

As for the relation of this science, or its standing in relation to the other sciences: it is the relation of "generality and particularity in a respect," because it shares with the science of hadith the study of chains and texts, and shares likewise with the science of hidden defects in these two matters, and shares with the principles of jurisprudence in the modes of derivation, and with jurisprudence as well — because documentation is for the most part directed upon the proofs for legal rulings. It is very rare that you find among people one who documents what concerns other than the proofs for rulings. True, there is no doubt that some people have documented certain things that have no direct relation to the proofs for rulings: for instance, the judge ʿIyad documented the hadith of Umm Zarʿ, and he did not intend documentation only, and for that reason he mentioned what is derived from it and named his book Bughyat al-Rāʾid li-mā Taḍammanahu Ḥadīth Umm Zarʿ min al-Fawāʾid. He mentioned its variant forms, and whether it is all of it raised to the Prophet, or whether the part raised to him is only "I am to you as Abu Zarʿ was to Umm Zarʿ, save that I shall not divorce you," or otherwise; and he confined its lines of transmission and then mentioned what is derived from it of useful points, and did well and gave benefit, may God have mercy on him.

Likewise the Hafiz Ibn Hajar, for instance, in the hadith "Do not revile my Companions," documented it in an independent fascicle, mentioning in it the lines of transmission of this hadith and attempting to cover them all.

Likewise al-Suyuti, in the mass-transmitted hadiths, attempted to cover some of the lines of transmission of certain hadiths, such as the hadith "May God make radiant a man who hears my words and retains them and conveys them as he heard them."

As for its ruling: the ruling of the science of documentation is that it is a collective obligation (farḍ kifāyah) upon other than the disputant. As for the disputant, it is incumbent upon him to know the rank of the hadith by which he disputes, because it is not lawful for him to ascribe to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, what he is not certain that he said. Hence the first hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, in its introduction, is that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever relates from me a hadith while he holds it to be a lie against me is one of the liars" — or "one of the two liars."

Its merit: it is according to the benefit derived from it, because the merit of every science is according to its benefit.

Its name: "documentation" (al-takhrīj). Its origin is from ikhrāj, bringing out, as though a man wishes that hadith to come out from his transmission so as to spread among people. Of the verb one says kharraja and akhraja, so one says: "Ahmad brought it out (akhraja) in the Musnad," and "Ahmad brought it out (kharraja) in the Musnad." But the later scholars have a particular convention, for al-Dimyati, may God have mercy on him, distinguishes between akhraja and kharraja: when he says akhraja, its meaning is that the hadith is of the kind by which one argues, acceptable, whether it be sound or good or otherwise; and when he says kharraja, its meaning is that the hadith is rejected and not to be argued by, being weak or forged. This is the difference between akhraja and kharraja — but it is a conventional difference, not a linguistic one.

The people of hadith, for their part, distinguish between al-istikhrāj and al-ikhrāj: al-ikhrāj is, as we mentioned, the mention of the hadith's lines of transmission, who transmitted it, its place, and the grading upon it; while al-istikhrāj is the mention of a line of transmission for the hadith other than the line of the author of the book — as we mentioned earlier under the mustakhrajāt.

With this we have come, in effect, to the end of the preliminaries of the science of documentation.

Question 1: We would like a comment on the methodology of authors in grading certain hadiths as sound or as weak, and likewise on the division of their personalities between strictness and laxity across their various compositions.

Answer: Our scholars, may God have mercy on them, did not have specialisation, as we mentioned before; rather their sciences were comprehensive sciences. So in studying jurisprudence a man relies, when he mentions a proof, on the fact that he will study it in another place; and when he studies it on the creedal side, for instance, he refers it to another place — and so on. For that reason references abound in their books. With many of our scholars, when you read for them you do not read a page without finding in it: "the exhaustive treatment of that is in another place," "we have treated that exhaustively elsewhere," "what is intended here — as Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah says," "we have set that out in a place more fully than here," "what is intended here is such-and-such." So they refer to their references because these are ready to hand with them. Hence if one of them is composing on jurisprudence, he may be lax in adducing some weak hadiths, following the jurists, because he is now in the realm of the jurists and travelling their road; whereas if he is composing on documentation and on hidden defects, he takes the exactness of the people of documentation and hidden defects. In this way he comes to have more than one personality. As for what occurs of some scholars' citing certain hadiths with a weakening in one place and a grading as sound in another, that is on account of an increase of knowledge: either by way of a genuine increase of knowledge, so that this is a retraction of the earlier grading; or it may be from forgetfulness, inattention and lapse of memory — and all of that is possible. Al-Suyuti, may God have mercy on him, is among those well known for this: he grades a hadith as sound in one of his books and then weakens it in another book, because of some fresh knowledge that came to him in the matter, or because in that book he intends to abridge particular books whose authors weaken this hadith, while in another place he simply follows those who mentioned it without qualification, or relies upon himself and grades it sound relying on his own information. Likewise in his citations from the imams this sort of thing often occurs — as in his citing from Malik, may God have mercy on him, that he held it forbidden to quote from the Book and the Sunnah in poetry. He cited this from him in Sharḥ ʿUqūd al-Jumān and cited the like of it from him also in al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, and then denied it with a flat denial in his commentary on the Muwaṭṭaʾ, Tanwīr al-Ḥawālik; and Tanwīr al-Ḥawālik is later in composition than the two earlier books. This is what my teacher Muhammad Salim put into verse when he said:

*What al-Jalal mentioned in al-Itqān, and in his ʿUqūd al-Jumān,*

*of the prohibition of quotation according to Malik — he said more in his Tanwīr al-Ḥawālik*

*in rejecting it, and in imputing empty talk to whoever pointed to holding it forbidden.*

*I say: and chronology, by the later date, gives judgment in favour of al-Tanwīr, the container of what is good.*

For this reason, what is done today by those who hunt out slips and search for them, studying the books of Shaykh al-Albani, for instance, in order to find in them a weakening of certain hadiths in one place and a grading of the same as sound in another — this is a crooked method. The grading as sound and the grading as weak are, in such a case, both of them built upon the change of a man's conviction according to his knowledge. ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "That was according to what we judged then, and this is according to what we judge now." A man is obliged to renew his independent reasoning in every matter and not to disdain returning to the truth. Hence ʿUmar wrote to Abu Musa in the letter on judgeship: "Let not a judgment you gave yesterday, and then reviewed within yourself and were guided in it to your right course, prevent you from returning to the truth; for the truth is ancient and nothing annuls it, and returning to the truth is better than persisting in falsehood."

As for people's methodologies, there is no doubt that modern scholarship today has produced methods that are for the most part regular; and if a man does not follow them in all his books, he at least keeps to them within the single book — as with academic theses today: if he violates his method even in the ordering of the positions, or in the discussion of the proofs, or otherwise, he is held to account for it, because he has changed the methodology. With the ancients, however, a change of methodology might be something they liked, and especially one who composes in grammar and rhetoric. The people of rhetoric prefer variation in the modes of expression to routine in them, because they hold that routine in them entails tedium, whereas variation in them is a fresh invention and an expression in differing modes. For this reason Ibn Malik, may God have mercy on him, in his Alfiyyah always pursues this rhetorical course. He said, for instance, in enumerating the separate pronouns:

*And among the pronouns of the nominative is that which lies concealed, as in "do," "I agree," "we rejoice" — when you give thanks.*

*And that which has the nominative in separation is anā, huwa and anta; and the derived forms are not obscure.*

*And that which is put in the accusative in separation is iyyāya; and the branching from it is not problematic.*

So he makes the syntactic ruling an adverbial qualifier in the last line, while in the line before it he makes the ruling itself the predicate and makes separation the adverbial qualifier — he varies the methodology accordingly.

As for one who occupies himself with documentation — with documenting any hadith — if he is an author writing for others, it does not suffice in his documentation that he should say "so-and-so graded it sound" or "so-and-so weakened it." This is not enough. It suffices only if he brings a large number of famous scholars who agreed in succession upon grading it sound: his own liability may be discharged if he says, "It was graded sound by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, the Hafiz Ibn Hajar, so-and-so and so-and-so" — counting a group; because it is not possible that all these should be among the lax and that error should befall them all. Even so, the safer course for him is always to search out his own conviction; and if the conviction arises in him, that suffices. There is no difference between his citing a grading of sound or weak and his citing the legal opinion of one of the scholars in a juristic question. Regrettably, many researchers in juristic questions turn aside from the position of Imam Ahmad and the position of Ibn Qudamah and the position of Ibn Taymiyyah and come with their own independent reasoning, while in documentation they say "al-Albani graded it sound" and are content with that. Why do you imitate blindly a person contemporary with you in one question, while in the other you repudiate imitation altogether, even of the great masters of independent reasoning?

Question 2: Why do the hadith scholars show laxity in the state of gathering, while in the state of transmitting they are strict?

Answer: The origin of that is that the people of hadith counsel the student of hadith, in the stage of seeking, to "gather indiscriminately" (al-taqmīsh), and in the stage of composing to "sift" (al-taftīsh). Hence al-ʿIraqi, may God have mercy on him, mentioned their saying:

*Gather when you read — gather, gather! Sift when you relate — sift, sift!*

In the state of gathering he "gathers indiscriminately" and collects everything, and in the state of composing and relating he "sifts."

Question 3: Does a divergence between theory and practice occur? And is there a distinction between questions of independent reasoning and questions of disagreement?

Answer: The important matter in this chapter is to know that the divergence between theory and practice does in fact occur, and many of the scholars whom people call the verifiers have noticed it. For instance, Ibn Nujaym of the Hanafis often comes with a correction: when the Hanafis lay down some rule, he comes and says, "Look at the confusion occurring in their words between the rule and its derived cases" — he means between theory and practice. Likewise Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah noticed a great difference between practice and the laying down of rules, and drew attention to it too in certain places.

Among the examples of divergence between practice and the laying down of rules, even in the ordinary juristic maxims, is the maxim "There is no censure in questions of disagreement." This is a maxim which the schools laid down, and they said that censure includes, for example, the annulling of a judgment. They said: the judgment of a judge is not annulled unless it contradicts a text from the Book or the Sunnah, or consensus, or plain analogy, or an accredited maxim…

*If a judge one day gives judgment in four things, the judgment is dissolved after having been made binding:*

*in contradiction of a text, of a consensus, of a maxim, and likewise of plain analogy — enough for you; understand.*

Al-Qarafi came and said: "These things mentioned must be qualified. If 'contradiction of a text' is said, what is meant by it is contradiction of a text free of any counter-evidence; and if 'the maxim' is said, what is meant is one free of counter-evidence; and if 'contradiction of plain analogy' is said, what is meant is one free of counter-evidence; and as for 'consensus,' what is meant by it is actual consensus and not tacit consensus — explicit consensus."

Ibn Taymiyyah came and qualified it with another qualification. He said: what is meant by their saying "There is no censure in questions of disagreement" is questions of independent reasoning; and not every disagreement is reckoned as valid, but only a disagreement that has a share of soundness in the view taken. From this it follows that in the non-ijtihadic questions, which are settled by strong texts, a judgment is annulled and the one who goes against them is censured.

Ibn al-Humam of the Hanafis came after Ibn Taymiyyah and made a further correction. He said: there is no sense in distinguishing between questions of independent reasoning and questions of disagreement! How do we know that a question is one of independent reasoning or is not, except by those who disagree over it? So if it is established that Abu Hanifah, al-Shafiʿi, Malik and Ahmad are men of independent reasoning, and they disagreed over a question, then we cannot but judge it to be among the questions of independent reasoning and among the questions of disagreement; and it is established that they are men of independent reasoning and of high standing, so that every matter over which they disagreed is open to independent reasoning. Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him, gave examples, among them, for instance, "marriage without a guardian." He said: this is among the questions of "disagreement" and not among the questions of "independent reasoning," because it is settled by the text. Ibn al-Humam answers him, saying: "This text is faced by another text." For you rely on the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ashʿari, "There is no marriage except with a guardian"; while we rely, in not making it a condition, upon the words of God Most High: {Do not prevent them from marrying their husbands when they have agreed together honourably} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:232). So the disagreement is not settled; the disagreement will always remain in existence.

So then, the divergence between theory and practice exists; and among the questions that follow from this is acting upon the weak hadith. Many of the people of knowledge, among them Imam al-Nawawi, and the Sultan of the Scholars al-ʿIzz ibn ʿAbd al-Salam, and al-Mundhiri, have mentioned "that the weak hadith may be acted upon in the merits of deeds," and they made this a maxim. But the difficulty comes when we come to application: what are the merits of deeds? And what do you mean by the merits of deeds? If what is meant by them is the recommended acts of prayer and the recommended acts of the pilgrimage, this will be legislation at its very core, and there will be in it innovations without beginning or end, exceedingly many. But if what is meant by the merits of deeds is the softening narratives and the moral qualities and the matter of renunciation, and what indicates an increase of reward in some matter, then this is an easy thing, because in that case they are not a proof of it. Among those who criticised this maxim and made observations upon it is Shaykh al-Albani, may God have mercy on him. He was much concerned with this maxim and was strict about it, and pressed his censure hard upon al-Nawawi and others, in the introduction to his book on the description of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and likewise in the introduction to the Silsilah — Silsilat al-Aḥādīth al-Ṣaḥīḥah. But the reality is that al-Albani approached it from the side of application, while the earlier scholars approached it from the laying down of the rule. For this reason a fair-minded student can combine their positions and find that the matter is easier than al-Albani, may God have mercy on him, made it out to be.

Question 4: We would like a statement of the importance of the chain of transmission, and what the standing is of books that are without chains.

Answer: As for the chain of transmission — as we mentioned before — it is "the lineage of the hadith; and were it not for the chain of transmission, whoever wished would say whatever he wished; and the chain of transmission is among the distinguishing features of the community of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace." The people of hadith say, "It is honour enough for a man that his name should be the lowest of a chain whose highest is the name of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace." It is a real connection — a spiritual connection by transmission between you and the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and between you and the people of knowledge from whom you transmit. For that reason it was not fitting for the community to be negligent of the chains of transmission, nor to abandon them.

As for our present reality, there is no doubt that many of the books that have reached us are not transmitted; and we mentioned before that many of the printings are not to be trusted, and we drew attention to many gross errors in them. So what is the solution? Many of those who make a profession of documentation in this age of ours rely upon a single manuscript existing in a library in the West, for example, and on that basis they consider a hadith sound or weak, relying on the fact that it is found in a book by Ibn Abi al-Dunya, or a book by Ibn Abi ʿAsim, that is not well known and not transmitted and is found in one of the manuscripts in Germany or Britain, or even in some of the Muslim countries. This is a great problem.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr and al-Suyuti spoke of it long ago. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: "The Sunnah is preserved as the Qur'an is preserved, because it is revelation. As for what has been forgotten of the compositions and the great books that have not reached us, its meaning is that the community has no need of them, so that they are like what has been abrogated; and for that reason burrowing after them and bringing them out anew is not required by the Law, and is among the self-imposed burdens in which there is no benefit." He held it to be like what is abrogated and what is caused to be forgotten: {Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or the like of it} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:106).

Al-Suyuti likewise spoke of this matter and mentioned "that what the generality of the community needs is present among the generality, and what the elect need is present among the elect." So, for instance, certain hadiths may be in rare books which not everyone needs; but the scholars and the masters have their hands reaching to them, or at the very least the hand of one by whom the proof is established in that chapter reaches them.

In general this matter is still a place of difficulty, because the hadith scholars count the relating of a hadith, or ascribing it to a book, without a man having a transmission of it, as among the "theft of hadith" for which a man is impugned. Many of the transmitters by reason of whom hadiths have been weakened were not weakened on account of religion or truthfulness, but were weakened on account of the theft of hadith — and they are a large number. Today most of the documenters are among the thieves of hadith: they have no transmission in these books. But it may be said that this sort of thing is among the cases in which recourse is had to taking comfort in the number of the recensions in existence. There is no doubt that confidence in a book of which twenty handwritten copies exist is stronger and greater than confidence in a book of which there is only one copy, copied from a microfilm, with much haziness and effacement in it. Regrettably, many editors photograph the manuscript, and then, when you go back to the very photograph by which they wished to establish the reading, you find that they have contradicted it in what they wrote. An example of that is the man who edited the book al-Muwaṭṭaʾ in the transmission of Abu Musʿab al-Zuhri in two volumes, which is printed and published. He photographed the first page of the manuscript he relied upon, and he wrote out the first hadith that Malik brought out in the Muwaṭṭaʾ, the hadith of al-Zuhri: "That ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz delayed the prayer one day while he was in Medina, and ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr came in to him and said: Do you not know that al-Mughirah ibn Shuʿbah delayed the prayer one day while he was in Kufa, and Abu Masʿud al-Badri came in to him and said: What is this, O Mughirah? (Do you not know that Gabriel came down and prayed, and the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, prayed; then he prayed, and the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, prayed; then he prayed, and the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, prayed; then he prayed, and the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, prayed; then he prayed, and the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, prayed; then he said: with this I was commanded)." The words "then he said: with this I was commanded" are perfectly clear in the manuscript, and they corrupted and disfigured them, putting in their place another word, remote, having no relation to the hadith and not transmitted at all.

As for the many editors who do not read the scripts, they are not to be trusted, because a man may find a manuscript in the Persian script while he is not proficient in this script, or in the Kufic script while he is not proficient in it, or in the Maghribi script while he is not proficient in it, and so he writes what contradicts what is in it — while you, when you look at it, find the truth plain in it.

Question 5: Can one who is not a specialist in documentation do documentation?

Answer: As for one who is not a specialist in documentation, he ought to go back to several references until his own conviction arises in him; and if he has no time for that, it is possible for him to ask directly — he asks one whose religion and knowledge he trusts, and so places the matter upon that man's neck, and he is the one answerable for it. This is what the people of knowledge used to do in earlier times. The "questionings" (suʾālāt), for instance, are numerous among the hadith scholars: there is now printed the Questionings of Abu Dawud to Imam Ahmad on hidden defects; the Questionings of al-Tirmidhi to al-Bukhari, which he brought in his ʿIlal: "I asked Muhammad" — that is al-Bukhari — "about this hadith, and he said: 'In it there is something to be considered'"; and likewise the questionings of a number of the imams to al-Daraqutni, the questionings of a number of the imams to Ibn Maʿin, and the questionings of Shaykh al-Salafi too to some of his teachers. These are all a well-known method in documentation: a person is not a specialist, or is still a student, and so he asks one who is stronger than he is and whose judgment he trusts.

As for today, God has also made easy these discs which gather many of the texts, so that recourse to them all at one time is made easy — even though in the printings themselves you find very gross errors; but in general you compare between them. We have been tried with this in many books: for instance the book al-Musnad by al-Tayalisi, which is the oldest Musnad we have today. All its printings contain errors past imagining, very gross errors; and we were tried with that, so we used to go back in it to al-Sunan al-Kubrā of al-Bayhaqi and find the hadith sound there — and it would be by intermediaries, of course, by way of descent, but al-Bayhaqi transmits it with his chain up to Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi. So the Musnad of al-Tayalisi is corrected from the Sunan of al-Bayhaqi; and likewise al-Mustadrak is corrected from the Sunan of al-Bayhaqi. The Sunan of al-Bayhaqi is a foundation from which what preceded it is corrected: every later book you treat as though it were a fresh recension of the books of the predecessors, and you go over what is in it.

In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate.

We have before us now the science of hidden defects (ʿilm al-ʿilal), and it likewise is one of the sciences that serve the Sunnah, one of the important sciences, which none dares to approach but the people of knowledge; it is not for the generality of people. In this science the skill of certain men has shown itself, men whom God, glorified and exalted, prepared to bear the responsibility of defending the Sunnah of His Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace — and they are the masters.

This science is the highest and most exacting thing the hadith scholars reached in the hadith sciences generally, and it is the material of the science of documentation.

Documentation, as we mentioned, is meant to give a grading upon a hadith, so that it may be known whether it remains on the roll of what rulings are derived from, or is set aside. The outcome of documentation is acceptance or rejection; and the material of that is "the hidden defects."

If we wish to define "the science of hidden defects," that is something difficult. A number of the imams were asked about it — about a comprehensive definition of it — and they were not able to produce one. Abu Hatim al-Razi was asked about the science of hidden defects: what is it? What is this "defect" that you speak of? He said: "If you ask me about a hadith and I say it has a hidden defect, then go to Abu Zurʿah and he will say it has a hidden defect; then go to Ibn Hanbal and he will say it has a hidden defect; then go to Yahya ibn Maʿin and he will say it has a hidden defect. And when you see that, know that it is 'a light which God places in the heart of whomever He wills of His servants.'"

This is not a definition of the science, but it shows us that "the science of hidden defects" is part of God's safeguarding — glorified and exalted is He — of His Law and His religion, and that it is a conviction arising in the hadith scholar of a weakness in the hadith, or a sickness in it. This sickness is of varied kinds, and this conviction arises only in one who is practised in hadith. For the practised man, the student of hadith, reaches a level at which the style of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, is not confused for him with the style of anyone else — like the people of rhetorical taste: when one of them specialises in a particular poet he knows whether these verses are of his poetry or are not of his poetry, because he knows his vocabulary and his language and his style and the meanings he broaches. So likewise the specialist in hadith, when he has absorbed many of the hadiths and been imprinted by them, knows what was from the lamp-niche of prophecy, as against what was transmitted according to sense, as against what has no basis at all.

From this we shall divide the hadith, from the standpoint of hidden defects, into three classes:

A hadith genuinely transmitted from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace — meaning that its wordings are from the wordings of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace.

The second level: what is similar to it — that is, its rulings are sound, belonging to the rulings of the Law, or may be sound, but its wordings are transmitted according to sense and are not from the wordings of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace; so its meanings are prophetic meanings, but its wordings are not so.

The third class: what is remote in both wording and meaning together from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace.

By this division it becomes plain that the definition we can arrive at for "the science of hidden defects" is to say: "It is the science by which one discovers what bears upon a hadith of what diminishes its probative force or weakens its transmission, among what is obscure." For the hidden defects are specific to what is obscure, and specific likewise to what diminishes probative force or weakens the transmission.

They divide into two divisions: into what relates to the chains of transmission and what relates to the texts. As for what relates to the chains, the matter in it is manageable, because it belongs to the science of transmission. You know, for instance, that a certain man related this hadith often from a certain man, but that in one of the sessions he inserted a person between himself and him, saying: "So-and-so related to me from so-and-so." You take notice — since you were not entirely at ease about this hadith in the first place — and so you say: so-and-so practised concealment of a defect in this hadith and dropped so-and-so from between so-and-so and so-and-so.

translator_notes: Qur'anic renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic text of the Qur'an.

This is tape SEVEN of the Sheikh's course on the Islamic religious sciences (see IDs 448-455 and 458, 461 for other tapes). It carries three sessions: the close of the survey of the commentaries on the hadith collections (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Sunan Abī Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah, the Musnad, al-Mustadrak, al-Bayhaqī and the books of legal rulings); the whole of the science of documentation (takhrīj) through its ten preliminaries, followed by five questions; and the opening of the science of hidden defects (ʿilm al-ʿilal), which breaks off.

Book titles are given in transliteration without italics or quotation marks, following the convention of the other records in this corpus; italics are reserved for verse. Where the Sheikh names a book only by a short form (al-Kitāb, al-Tanqīḥ, al-Tuḥfah, al-Irwāʾ) the short form is kept, because his listeners are expected to know it and expanding it would put knowledge into his mouth.

The Sheikh numbers the five questions of the second session explicitly in the source (السؤال1 … السؤال5), and the English carries those numbers. No headings have been added that he does not speak; the two rules of dots are the source's own.
